sectors.name: Programming & CS Fundamentals
sectors.tagline: Start here: learn to think like a programmer before choosing a career path.
sectors.overview: Every tech career is built on the same base: logic, a first programming language, data structures, algorithms and how computers work. If you are not sure where to start, start here.
who_is_this_for: Absolute beginners who have never written code
Students who want a strong base before choosing a field
Anyone preparing for coding interviews
why_learn: Makes every other roadmap easier
Helps you crack coding interviews
Teaches you how to break big problems into small steps
what_you_will_build: A simple calculator and a number-guessing game
Your own implementations of lists, stacks and sorting
how_to_start: Open pythontutor.com and watch how a small Python program runs step by step.
Install Python from python.org and write a program that prints your name.
Start CS50P or Python for Everybody and solve one small problem every day.

glossary.meaning: A step-by-step recipe to solve a problem.
A named box that stores a value.
A reusable block of code that does one job.
A way to organise data, such as a list or a dictionary.
A way to describe how slow or fast code becomes as data grows.
Finding and fixing mistakes in code.

faq.question: Which language should I learn first?
faq.answer: Python is the easiest choice for beginners. The ideas you learn work in every language.

faq.question: Is DSA really needed?
faq.answer: Yes, for interviews and for writing efficient code. Start slowly after you know the basics.

faq.question: I get stuck a lot. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes. Getting stuck and solving it is how programmers learn.

faq.question: How many hours should I practise?
faq.answer: One focused hour every day beats seven hours once a week.

steps.title: Think Like a Programmer
steps.simple_explanation: Programming is just giving clear instructions. First learn to break a problem into small steps.
topics: Binary and how computers store data
steps.learning_outcome: Describe a solution step by step before writing code.
projects: Flowchart for making tea or logging into a website
Pseudocode for finding the biggest number in a list

steps.title: Your First Language: Python
steps.simple_explanation: Python reads almost like English, so it is the friendliest way to start coding.
steps.learning_outcome: Write real programs that solve everyday problems.

steps.title: Practise Problem Solving
steps.simple_explanation: Coding is a skill like football: you get better by playing small matches every day.
steps.learning_outcome: Solve easy coding problems without looking at the answer.

steps.title: Git and the Command Line
steps.simple_explanation: The terminal and Git are everyday tools for every developer.
steps.learning_outcome: Save and share your code like a professional.

steps.title: Data Structures
steps.simple_explanation: Data structures are different ways to store data so your program can find and change it quickly.
steps.learning_outcome: Choose the right data structure for a problem.
projects: Implement a stack and a queue
Build a simple autocomplete with a trie

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.simple_explanation: Algorithms are proven methods for searching, sorting and solving problems efficiently.
steps.learning_outcome: Solve medium-level interview problems with confidence.

steps.title: How Computers Really Work
steps.simple_explanation: Learn what happens inside the computer when your code runs: memory, processes, files and networks.
steps.learning_outcome: Understand the machine behind your code.
projects: Draw how a program runs in memory

steps.title: Choose Your Specialisation
steps.simple_explanation: Now you know the basics. Try small projects in different fields and pick the one you enjoy most.
steps.learning_outcome: Pick a path and follow its roadmap.
projects: Build one tiny project in 3 different fields

sectors.name: Web Development
sectors.tagline: Learn to build websites and web apps that anyone can open in a browser.
sectors.overview: Every website you use, from YouTube to your bank, is built by web developers. This path takes you from 'what is a browser?' to launching your own full-stack web app with login, database and hosting.
who_is_this_for: Complete beginners with no coding background
Students who want to build websites, portfolios or startups
Anyone who wants freelance or remote work
why_learn: Huge demand: almost every company needs a website or web app
You can start freelancing after a few months of practice
Skills transfer easily to mobile apps and software engineering
what_you_will_build: A to-do app, a weather app and a blog
A full-stack app with login and database
how_to_start: Install VS Code and Google Chrome (both free).
Create a file named index.html, write 'Hello World' in it and open it in your browser.
Follow the first lesson of freeCodeCamp Responsive Web Design and code for 30 minutes every day.

glossary.meaning: The language that gives a web page its structure, like the skeleton of a body.
The language that styles a page: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
The programming language that makes pages interactive.
A way for two programs to talk to each other and share data.
A ready-made toolkit that helps you build apps faster, for example React.
Putting your website on the internet so everyone can visit it.

faq.question: Do I need a powerful computer?
faq.answer: No. Any laptop that can run a browser and VS Code is enough.

faq.question: Do I need to be good at maths?
faq.answer: No. Basic logic is enough for web development.

faq.question: How long until I can get a job or client?
faq.answer: Most dedicated learners can build job-ready projects in 8 to 12 months with daily practice.

faq.question: Should I learn React first?
faq.answer: No. Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript properly first. React is much easier after that.

steps.title: How the Internet and the Web Work
steps.simple_explanation: Before building websites, understand what happens when you type a web address and press Enter.
steps.learning_outcome: Explain in simple words how a website reaches your screen.
projects: Draw the journey of one web request on paper
Write a short note: 'What happens when I open google.com?'

steps.title: HTML: The Structure of a Page
steps.simple_explanation: HTML is how you tell the browser: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is an image.
steps.learning_outcome: Build well-structured, accessible web pages from scratch.

steps.title: CSS: Style and Layout
steps.simple_explanation: CSS makes a plain page beautiful and makes it work on phones, tablets and big screens.
steps.learning_outcome: Create attractive, responsive layouts that work on any screen.

steps.title: JavaScript: Make Pages Interactive
steps.simple_explanation: JavaScript is a real programming language. It lets buttons click, forms validate and data load without refreshing.
steps.learning_outcome: Build interactive apps and fetch data from APIs.

steps.title: Git, GitHub and Developer Tools
steps.simple_explanation: Git saves every version of your code like a time machine. GitHub is where you store it online and show it to the world.
steps.learning_outcome: Track your code, publish projects on GitHub and debug in the browser.
projects: Upload all your projects to GitHub
Contribute a small fix to an open-source repo

steps.title: React and TypeScript
steps.simple_explanation: React helps you build big interfaces from small reusable pieces called components. TypeScript adds safety by catching mistakes early.
steps.learning_outcome: Build modern single-page applications with clean, typed code.

steps.title: Frontend Pro: Accessibility, Performance and State
steps.simple_explanation: Make your interfaces fast, usable by everyone and ready for real products used by thousands of people.
topics: Forms and validation (React Hook Form, Zod)
steps.learning_outcome: Build production-quality, accessible and fast frontends.
projects: Next.js blog with SEO and a 90+ Lighthouse score

steps.title: Backend: Node.js, Express and APIs
steps.simple_explanation: The backend is the hidden part of a website that stores data, checks passwords and sends information to the frontend.
steps.learning_outcome: Create secure APIs that your frontend can use.

steps.title: Backend Pro: Security, Caching and Architecture
steps.simple_explanation: Learn what separates a toy API from a safe, fast and well-organised backend that real companies run.
steps.learning_outcome: Design secure, well-structured and fast backend services.
projects: API with roles, rate limiting and docs

steps.title: Databases and Next.js Full-Stack
steps.simple_explanation: A database is the long-term memory of your app. Next.js lets you build frontend and backend together in one project.
steps.learning_outcome: Build complete full-stack apps with real data.

steps.title: Testing, Security, Deployment and Performance
steps.simple_explanation: Real products must be tested, safe, fast and online. This step turns your project into something professional.
topics: Deploy on Vercel or a VPS
steps.learning_outcome: Ship a production-ready web application.
projects: Deploy your full-stack app with a custom domain
Add automated tests and a CI pipeline

steps.title: Portfolio, Interviews and Career
steps.simple_explanation: Show your work, practise interview questions and start earning from your skills.
steps.learning_outcome: Be ready to apply for jobs and freelance projects.

tracks.name: Frontend Developer
tracks.tagline: Build what users see and touch.
tracks.summary: Frontend developers create the pages, buttons, animations and layouts people use every day. You will master HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React and TypeScript, then learn accessibility, performance and Next.js. You can skip the heavy backend steps.

tracks.name: Backend Developer
tracks.tagline: Build the engine behind every app.
tracks.summary: Backend developers build servers, APIs, databases and security. You will learn the web basics, JavaScript, Node.js, authentication, caching and databases, and you can skip the design-heavy frontend steps.

tracks.name: Full Stack Developer
tracks.tagline: Build complete products from start to finish.
tracks.summary: Full stack developers work on both the frontend and the backend. This is the longest path, but it lets you build and launch whole products alone, which is great for freelancing and startups.

sectors.name: Software Engineering
sectors.tagline: Learn how professional teams design, build, test and maintain software.
sectors.overview: Writing code is only one part of software engineering. You also learn to plan, design clean systems, work in teams, test your work and keep software running for years.
who_is_this_for: Beginners who know basic programming
Students who want to work in a software company
Developers who want to move from 'coding' to 'engineering'
why_learn: Software engineers are needed in every industry
Good design skills make you valuable in any team
Clear path to senior and lead roles
what_you_will_build: A clean, tested project with documentation
A team project using Git and pull requests
prerequisites: One programming language (Python, Java or JavaScript)
how_to_start: Pick one language and finish one small project in it.
Read the first chapter of Refactoring Guru's design patterns.
Create a GitHub repository and write a good README for it.

glossary.meaning: Code that is easy for other people to read and change.
Improving code structure without changing what it does.
A proven solution to a common design problem.
A small automatic check that one piece of code works.
Automatic testing and delivery of code after every change.
A small independent service that does one job in a bigger system.

faq.question: Is software engineering different from programming?
faq.answer: Yes. Programming writes code. Engineering also covers design, testing, teamwork and maintenance.

faq.question: Do I need a degree?
faq.answer: A degree helps, but strong projects and skills matter most.

faq.question: Which language is best?
faq.answer: Any mainstream language works. Learn concepts deeply and they transfer.

faq.question: How do I get real experience?
faq.answer: Contribute to open source and build team projects with code reviews.

steps.title: Programming Strength
steps.simple_explanation: Be comfortable in one language and know how to solve problems with it.
topics: One language deeply (Python, Java or JS)
steps.learning_outcome: Write correct, readable programs on your own.

steps.title: Version Control and Team Workflow
steps.simple_explanation: Teams never email code. They use Git branches and pull requests to work together safely.
steps.learning_outcome: Collaborate on code without breaking each other's work.
projects: Make a team project with 2 friends
Open one pull request on an open-source repo

steps.title: Clean Code and Refactoring
steps.simple_explanation: Code is read many more times than it is written. Make it easy to understand.
steps.learning_outcome: Turn messy code into clean, maintainable code.
projects: Refactor an old project of yours
Write a code-style guide for a team

steps.title: Design Patterns and Architecture
steps.simple_explanation: Patterns are tested ideas that save you from re-inventing solutions.
steps.learning_outcome: Design flexible software structure before coding.

steps.title: Testing and Quality
steps.simple_explanation: Tests are a safety net. They let you change code without fear.
steps.learning_outcome: Write reliable tests for every project.
projects: Add 80% test coverage to a project

steps.title: Databases, APIs and Backend Systems
steps.simple_explanation: Most real software stores data and offers APIs to other apps.
steps.learning_outcome: Build backend services with data and APIs.

steps.title: System Design
steps.simple_explanation: Learn how big products like Facebook or Uber handle millions of users.
steps.learning_outcome: Design large systems on a whiteboard and explain the trade-offs.
projects: Design a chat app and a news feed

steps.title: DevOps, CI/CD and Delivery
steps.simple_explanation: Ship small changes safely and often with automation.
steps.learning_outcome: Automate build, test and deploy.
projects: CI pipeline that tests and deploys on every push

steps.title: Agile, Teamwork and Career
steps.simple_explanation: Software is built by teams. Communication matters as much as code.
steps.learning_outcome: Work smoothly in a professional team and pass interviews.
projects: Write a design document for your project

sectors.name: App Development
sectors.tagline: Build apps for Android and iPhone that people install and use daily.
sectors.overview: Mobile apps are used for banking, shopping, learning, entertainment and more. This path teaches you to build real Android, iOS and cross-platform apps and publish them to the app stores.
who_is_this_for: Beginners who want to build phone apps
Web developers moving to mobile
Students who want to publish their own app
why_learn: Everyone has a smartphone, so apps reach huge audiences
High demand for Flutter, React Native and Kotlin developers
You can publish your own product and earn from it
what_you_will_build: A weather and news app with APIs
A chat or social app with login
A published app on Google Play
prerequisites: A computer able to run Android Studio (8 GB RAM recommended)
how_to_start: Install Flutter or Android Studio following the official guide.
Run the default sample app on an emulator or your own phone.
Change the text and colour of the sample app to see how code changes the screen.

glossary.meaning: A small building block of a screen, like a button or a text box.
The data that changes while an app is running.
A virtual phone that runs on your computer.
A way for your app to get data from a server.
An app made for only one platform, such as Android.
One codebase that runs on both Android and iOS.

faq.question: Android, iOS or Flutter first?
faq.answer: Flutter is a great start because one codebase makes both Android and iOS apps.

faq.question: Do I need a Mac?
faq.answer: Only to build and publish iOS apps. Android and Flutter work on Windows or Linux.

faq.question: Do I need to know web development?
faq.answer: No, but basic programming knowledge helps a lot.

faq.question: Can I earn from apps?
faq.answer: Yes, through freelancing, jobs, ads, subscriptions or your own products.

steps.title: Mobile and Programming Basics
steps.simple_explanation: Learn the language your app will be written in and how phone apps are organised.
steps.learning_outcome: Write basic programs in Dart or Kotlin.

steps.title: Build Your First Screens
steps.simple_explanation: Everything on a phone screen is made of small pieces called widgets or composables.
steps.learning_outcome: Create beautiful multi-screen apps.

steps.title: State Management and Logic
steps.simple_explanation: State is the live data of your app, like the items in a cart. Managing it well keeps apps clean.
steps.learning_outcome: Keep app data organised and predictable.

steps.title: APIs and Local Storage
steps.simple_explanation: Most apps show data from the internet and save some data on the phone.
steps.learning_outcome: Connect apps to servers and save data offline.

steps.title: Firebase, Authentication and Notifications
steps.simple_explanation: Firebase gives you login, a database, file storage and notifications without building a server.
steps.learning_outcome: Add real accounts, cloud data and notifications.

steps.title: Native Features and Device Access
steps.simple_explanation: Phones have cameras, GPS and sensors. Great apps use them.
steps.learning_outcome: Use phone hardware safely inside your app.

steps.title: Quality, Performance and Design Polish
steps.simple_explanation: Users delete slow or confusing apps. Polish makes the difference.
steps.learning_outcome: Build fast, accessible and well-designed apps.
projects: Add tests and dark mode to an old app
Fix performance issues with the profiler

steps.title: Publishing and Growth
steps.simple_explanation: Release your app to the world and learn from real users.
steps.learning_outcome: Publish an app and update it from user feedback.
projects: Publish your app on Google Play
Collect and fix 5 user bug reports

sectors.name: AI & Machine Learning
sectors.tagline: Teach computers to learn from data, see, read and make decisions.
sectors.overview: AI powers recommendations, chatbots, face unlock and self-driving cars. This path takes you from Python and maths basics to training your own models and deploying them.
who_is_this_for: Beginners curious about AI
Students who like maths, data and problem solving
Developers who want to add AI to their products
why_learn: One of the fastest-growing fields
AI skills improve almost every other tech career
You can build smart tools that save people time
what_you_will_build: A chatbot or small AI assistant
how_to_start: Open Google Colab (free) and run your first Python cell.
Watch 3Blue1Brown's neural network videos for the big picture.
Start Kaggle Learn: Python, then Pandas, then Intro to Machine Learning.

glossary.meaning: A program that has learned patterns from data.
Showing a model lots of examples so it can learn.
One piece of information used to make a prediction, like house size.
When a model memorises training data and fails on new data.
A model inspired by the brain, made of layers of simple units.
A large language model such as the one behind AI chatbots.

faq.question: Do I need advanced maths?
faq.answer: You need basic linear algebra, probability and a little calculus. You learn them step by step here.

faq.question: Do I need a GPU?
faq.answer: No. Google Colab and Kaggle give free GPUs to beginners.

faq.question: ML or deep learning first?
faq.answer: Classic ML first. It teaches the ideas that deep learning builds on.

faq.question: Can I get a job without a master's degree?
faq.answer: Yes, with strong projects, but research roles often prefer advanced degrees.

steps.title: Python and Tools
steps.simple_explanation: Python is the main language of AI. Learn it along with the notebook tools experts use.
steps.learning_outcome: Write Python to load, clean and explore data.
projects: Analyse a CSV of your own

steps.title: Maths You Really Need
steps.simple_explanation: Maths explains why models work. You only need a few core ideas.
steps.learning_outcome: Understand the numbers behind ML.
projects: Plot a function and its slope

steps.title: Classic Machine Learning
steps.simple_explanation: Teach a computer to predict, such as house prices or whether an email is spam.
steps.learning_outcome: Train and evaluate models with scikit-learn.

steps.title: Feature Engineering and Real Projects
steps.simple_explanation: Good data often beats fancy models. Learn to prepare it well.
steps.learning_outcome: Prepare messy real-world data for models.

steps.title: Deep Learning
steps.simple_explanation: Deep learning uses many layers of artificial neurons to learn complex patterns.
steps.learning_outcome: Build and train neural networks.

resources.name: Karpathy: Neural Networks Zero to Hero

steps.title: Transformers, LLMs and Generative AI
steps.simple_explanation: Transformers power ChatGPT-like tools. Learn how they work and how to use them.
steps.learning_outcome: Build apps on top of language models.

steps.title: MLOps and Deployment
steps.simple_explanation: A model is useful only when other people can use it.
steps.learning_outcome: Ship and monitor models in production.
projects: Deploy a model as a web API

steps.title: Specialise, Research and Career
steps.simple_explanation: Pick an area, read papers and build a strong portfolio.
steps.learning_outcome: Show deep skill in one AI area.
projects: Write a blog post explaining a paper

resources.description: Short free practical courses with notebooks.

sectors.final_project: Build and deploy an end-to-end AI product, for example a document question-answering assistant with a web interface, evaluation results and a public demo.

tracks.name: Machine Learning Engineer
tracks.tagline: Train, evaluate and ship classic and deep learning models.
tracks.summary: This track focuses on data, classic machine learning, feature engineering, deep learning and MLOps. It is the strongest base for ML engineer, data scientist and research roles. You can skip the language-model step for now and come back to it later.

tracks.name: LLM & GenAI Engineer
tracks.tagline: Build products on top of language models.
tracks.summary: This track goes quickly from Python and core ML to deep learning, transformers, prompt engineering, RAG and agents. It is the fastest path to building AI assistants and chatbots. Feature engineering is skipped here, so return to it if you move toward classic ML.

sectors.name: Data Science
sectors.tagline: Turn raw numbers into answers, charts and smart decisions.
sectors.overview: Data scientists find patterns in data to help companies decide what to do next. You will learn Excel, SQL, Python, statistics, visualisation and machine learning.
who_is_this_for: Beginners who like numbers and puzzles
Students who want an analyst or data science career
Professionals who want data-driven decisions
why_learn: Every business collects data and needs people to understand it
Entry roles like Data Analyst are friendly to beginners
Opens the door to AI and machine learning
what_you_will_build: A SQL analysis of a real dataset
A predictive model with a written report
prerequisites: No coding needed at the start
how_to_start: Open Google Sheets and make a simple chart from your own monthly expenses.
Do the first SQLBolt lessons (30 minutes).
Join the free Kaggle Learn Python course.

glossary.meaning: A collection of data, like a spreadsheet.
Fixing missing, wrong or duplicate data.
The language used to ask questions of databases.
Charts and graphs that explain data.
When two things tend to change together.
One screen showing key numbers and charts.

faq.question: Data analyst or data scientist?
faq.answer: Analysts explain what happened. Scientists also predict what will happen. Start as an analyst.

faq.question: Is coding required?
faq.answer: Yes, mainly SQL and Python, but you learn them step by step.

faq.question: Do I need strong maths?
faq.answer: School-level maths plus basic statistics is enough to begin.

faq.question: What is the first thing to learn?
faq.answer: Excel or Sheets, then SQL. They are used in almost every data job.

steps.learning_outcome: Make decisions backed by evidence.

steps.simple_explanation: A good chart helps people understand in seconds.
steps.learning_outcome: Build clear dashboards and reports.

steps.title: Machine Learning for Data Science

steps.learning_outcome: Build and explain predictive models.

steps.learning_outcome: Understand how data flows from source to dashboard.
projects: Model data in a warehouse with dbt

steps.title: Portfolio, Communication and Career
steps.simple_explanation: Employers hire people who can explain results simply.
steps.learning_outcome: Present your work and apply for roles.

sectors.name: Cyber Security
sectors.tagline: Learn to protect systems, networks and people from hackers.
sectors.overview: Cyber security experts defend websites, apps and networks. You will learn how computers and networks work, how attacks happen, and how to find and fix weaknesses legally and ethically.
who_is_this_for: Beginners curious about hacking and safety
Students who like puzzles and investigation
IT staff who want to move into security
why_learn: Very high demand and strong salaries worldwide
Mission-driven work protecting people and businesses
Many paths: defence, testing, forensics, cloud security
what_you_will_build: A home lab with safe vulnerable machines

Create a free TryHackMe account and finish the 'Pre Security' path.
Learn the 10 most common Linux commands.

glossary.meaning: A weakness that an attacker could use.
